meta.tagline: France's stomach capital: two rivers, one hill, a thousand bouchons

overview.title: Welcome to Lyon
overview.intro: Lyon is a city that doesn't try to prove itself; it doesn't need to. Two thousand years of Roman history, two rivers (the Rhône and the Saône), the silk-weavers' hill and the world's densest fabric of good restaurants speak for themselves. In place of Parisian polish, Lyon carries a well-fed self-assurance: at the table, in the street, in the hidden passageways. The French say you go to Lyon to eat; go — but don't bring only your appetite, for the city feeds the eyes too.

local_word.definition: Lyon's traditional eating house: checked tablecloths, elbow-to-elbow tables, robust home cooking, and a patron who knows what everyone is eating. Not Michelin polish but Lyonnais warmth; the city's culinary soul lives in these little dining rooms.

rules.title: A bouchon without a booking is a gamble
rules.description: Real bouchons are small and locals fill them; your odds of walking in at dinner are poor. Reserve by phone a day ahead, or book lunch as you pass the door.

rules.title: A traboule door is pushed, not shouted through
rules.description: The hidden passageways of Vieux Lyon and Croix-Rousse run through private buildings: push the door, pass quietly if it opens, leave the lights, keep your voice down. This is not a museum — people live here.

rules.title: Give Sunday morning to the markets
rules.description: The Saint-Antoine market on the Saône and the covered Halles de Lyon are the city's true museums; talk to the cheesemonger, ask for a taste, have breakfast at the counter.

tip.label: The Lyon philosophy
tip.text: The Lyonnais speak little and eat well. If you've sat at a table for two hours, the wine jug has been refilled, and the patron has called you 'mon ami': the city has accepted you.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Two rivers, two hills, one peninsula: crack Lyon's geography and you've cracked its transport.

items.title: Arrival — TGV and Rhônexpress
items.description: Two hours from Paris by TGV into Part-Dieu station; the Rhônexpress tram runs from the airport to the centre in 30 minutes. From Part-Dieu the metro takes you anywhere.

items.title: Metro, tram and funicular
items.description: The TCL network weaves the city with four metro lines and trams; the same ticket covers the funicular (the 'ficelle') up to Fourvière. The 24-hour pass is the traveller's friend.

items.title: The Presqu'île on foot
items.description: The peninsula between the rivers — Bellecour to Terreaux — walks end to end; the finest shopfronts and passages line this axis.

items.title: Vélo'v bikes
items.description: The city's shared bicycles are made for the riverbanks: the Rhône quay's bike path runs the city's whole length.

items.title: Vaporetto on the river
items.description: The river shuttle down the Saône to Confluence is transport and scenic cruise in one; float your way back from the museum.

callout.label: Funicular tip
callout.text: Ride the funicular up to Fourvière but walk down through the Roman theatres: a two-thousand-year-old staircase with the city as backdrop.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Lyon, which bank of which river you sleep on decides which character of the city you live.

local_word.definition: 'Almost-island': the city centre caught between the Rhône and the Saône. Lyon's shop window, bazaar and salon; if your address is here, everything is within walking distance.

items.name: Presqu'île — Bellecour/Terreaux
items.description: Among the squares, shops, opera and restaurants: the unfailing address for a first visit. The Bellecour end is calm and elegant, the Terreaux end young and lively.

items.name: Vieux Lyon — Renaissance lanes
items.description: The UNESCO-protected Renaissance quarter: traboule doors, cobblestones, bouchon lanterns. Tourist-heavy by day but magical at dawn and night; for those who want to sleep inside history.

items.name: Croix-Rousse — the silk-weavers' hill
items.description: The old silk-weavers' quarter is now Lyon's village-souled neighbourhood: morning market, sloping streets, bohemian cafés. Funicular to the centre, or a lovely downhill walk.

items.name: Left bank of the Rhône — Part-Dieu/Brotteaux
items.description: The station and business side: broad boulevards, the Halles de Lyon and reasonable hotels. Sensible for train connections and lovers of a Halles breakfast.

items.name: Confluence — new Lyon
items.description: The glass-and-steel new quarter at the meeting of the rivers: design hotels, the museum and quayside walks. Far from classic Lyon's fabric, but inspiring for architecture lovers.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Lyon sets the table in all four seasons; in December, the city's light literally shines.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Riverbank Season
items.subtitle: Spring · Quay walks, open terraces
items.description: The Rhône quay comes back to life: joggers, picnickers, river barges turned bars. The weather is ideal for eating your way around on foot, and tourist density is low.

callout.label: May tip
callout.text: In May the 'Nuits Sonores' electronic music festival sweeps the city; even non-listeners profit from the street energy.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Summer in a Roman Theatre
items.subtitle: Summer · Open-air concerts, long evenings
items.description: The 'Nuits de Fourvière' festival in the ancient theatre: concerts and cinema on two-thousand-year-old stone. In August the locals go on holiday and some bouchons close — the city is calm but slow.

callout.label: August note
callout.text: In mid-August a share of the famous tables take their annual leave; phone ahead to confirm your bouchon is open.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Peak of the Table
items.subtitle: Autumn · New season menus, Beaujolais
items.description: The food city's true season: game and mushrooms land on the menus, and on the third Thursday of November the Beaujolais Nouveau corks pop. In cool weather the warmth of a bouchon doubles.

callout.label: November tip
callout.text: Beaujolais Nouveau night (the 3rd Thursday of November) is a citywide celebration; make no plans that evening — surrender to the street.

items.label: Winter
items.name: City of Lights
items.subtitle: Winter · Fête des Lumières, misty rivers
items.description: For four nights around December 8, Lyon becomes the world's capital of light: buildings turn into canvases, squares into installations. The year's most crowded and most unforgettable stretch; January and February leave a misty, calm, well-fed city behind.

callout.label: December warning
callout.text: Finding a hotel for the Fête des Lumières is the year's hardest task; book months ahead or day-trip the festival from a neighbouring city.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: In Lyon, eating is not a tourist activity but the city's reason for being. Sit down at the table; the city handles the rest.

local_word.definition: The silk-workers' morning feast: charcuterie, offal and a glass of Beaujolais at the crack of dawn. The most local medal a brave traveller can earn in Lyon is that glass drunk at 9 am.

items.name: Quenelle de brochet
items.description: A pillow-soft dumpling of pike, at its peak with crayfish sauce Nantua — the summit of the Lyon classics. It looks light and fills you up; the test dish of any bouchon.

items.name: The offal courage league
items.description: Tablier de sapeur (tripe), andouillette (chitterling sausage), foie de veau: Lyonnais cooking honours the whole animal. Order to the measure of your courage; the patron will explain the rest.
items.tag: For the brave · ask at a bouchon

items.name: Rosette and saucisson brioché
items.description: Lyon's charcuterie pride: thin-sliced rosette and hot sausage baked in brioche. Cornerstones of the aperitif and the mâchon alike.

items.name: Saint-Marcellin and cervelle de canut
items.description: The Halles' ripened Saint-Marcellin is eaten with a spoon; the herbed fresh cheese called 'the silk-weaver's brain' is bread's best friend.
items.tag: Cheese counter · ask for it ripe

items.name: Beaujolais and Côtes du Rhône
items.description: The city's two rivers are made of wine: the fruit of Beaujolais from the north, the body of the Rhône from the south. In a bouchon it comes by the jug (the pot lyonnais, 46 cl) — no bottle required.

items.name: Praline pastries
items.description: Sugar-coated pink almonds are the signature of Lyon's pâtisserie: praline tart and praline brioche paint the bakery windows pink. A slice with coffee, a box for the suitcase.

callout.label: The bouchon rule
callout.text: Telling a real bouchon from a tourist imitation is easy: the real one has a short handwritten menu, the 'Les Bouchons Lyonnais' certificate at the door, and the patron in the dining room.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Gems
hidden_gems.intro: Lyon keeps its secrets behind walls — often literally. These six belong to those who push the door.

items.name: Traboule de la Cour des Voraces
items.description: Croix-Rousse's famous courtyard: a six-storey giant staircase that hosted the silk-workers' uprisings. Push the door, pass quietly — history lives in the stairwell.

items.name: Fresque des Lyonnais
items.description: An 800 m² mural on the Saône bank: Lyon's famous look out from painted windows — including Saint-Exupéry of Little Prince fame and chef Paul Bocuse. The city's letter to itself.

items.name: The Odeon beside the Fourvière theatre
items.description: In the great theatre's shadow, the small Odeon with its mosaic floor escapes most visitors; sit on the steps and test the two-thousand-year-old acoustics with your own voice.

items.name: Maison des Canuts
items.description: Jacquard looms still working in Croix-Rousse: the silk-masters' heirs demonstrate and explain. The shortest route to understanding Lyon's 'canut' soul.

items.name: Quai Saint-Antoine mornings
items.description: The Saône-bank market stalls on weekend mornings are the city's true pulse: cheese, oysters, flowers and river mist. Breakfast from the stalls, coffee on the quay.

items.name: Jardin des Curiosités
items.description: The little-known terrace garden on the Saint-Just hill: from its metal chairs — a gift from Montreal — the city spreads out like a scale model. Solitude guaranteed at sunset.

callout.label: Traboule tip
callout.text: Most traboule doors are open early morning and locked at night; the best exploring hours are 8–10 am. Pick up the free traboule map from the Vieux Lyon tourist office.

traps.title: Skip the Traps
traps.intro: Lyon is an honest city, but a few imitations circle its famous kitchen. Know these four and your table is guaranteed.

items.name: The 'tourist bouchons' of Rue Saint-Jean
items.description: On Vieux Lyon's main street, imitators drape checked cloths and hang photo menus, selling frozen quenelle at bouchon prices.
items.instead: Look for the certificate ('Les Bouchons Lyonnais') or step one street back; in doubt, check lunchtime — a real bouchon is full of locals at noon.

items.name: The sit-down surprise at the Halles
items.description: The Halles de Lyon is an elegant covered market; at some counter-restaurants, table service costs distinctly more than the counter.
items.instead: Read the price list before sitting; or buy at the counter and eat on the quay — oysters open just as well outdoors.

items.name: Ferris-wheel tourism on Bellecour
items.description: The wheel and souvenir stands on the square collect time and money; Lyon's views are free from its hills anyway.
items.instead: The Fourvière terrace and the Croix-Rousse slopes give the best panoramas for nothing; leave the wheel to the kids.

items.name: A haggled taxi from the airport
items.description: A taxi from Saint-Exupéry to the centre costs seriously; the unlicensed drivers promising a 'flat rate' want even more.
items.instead: The Rhônexpress reaches Part-Dieu in 30 minutes; in a group, confirm the official taxi fare before boarding.

callout.label: The golden rule
callout.text: Three signs of a good table in Lyon: a short menu, a full room, a talkative patron. If all three are present, think of your appetite, not your wallet.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: Hill, traboule and bouchon — Lyon in summary

steps.title: Croix-Rousse market
steps.description: Cheese and fruit at the hilltop morning market; coffee on the square, catching the village rhythm of the silk-weavers' quarter.

steps.title: The traboule descent
steps.description: Start at the Cour des Voraces and drop down the slope through hidden passages: every door a surprise, every courtyard a century.

steps.title: Lunch at a bouchon
steps.description: At your reserved table: quenelle or tablier de sapeur, Beaujolais by the pot. Hurrying forbidden.

steps.title: Vieux Lyon + the cathedral
steps.description: Walk the Renaissance lanes, enter Saint-Jean with its astronomical clock; an ice-cream stop is permitted.

steps.title: Funicular to Fourvière
steps.description: From the basilica's terrace, the two-rivered city lies at your feet; make the descent through the Roman theatres.

steps.title: Evening on the Rhône quay
steps.description: A glass on the river barges, then dinner on the Presqu'île; let the table run long — Lyon likes it that way.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the city as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: Classic Lyon
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: Croix-Rousse, traboules, bouchon, Fourvière.

steps.title: Table and art
steps.description: A counter tour of the Halles de Lyon in the morning (Saint-Marcellin + oysters), the Museum of Fine Arts or Confluence in the afternoon, a cheese board in the Beaujolais bars at night.

steps.title: Rivers and goodbye
steps.description: The Saint-Antoine market in the morning, a Vélo'v pedal to the Tête d'Or park, the Fresque des Lyonnais and a last traboule or two in the afternoon; for the farewell dinner — this time order the bravest thing on the menu.

phrases.title: The 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: French courtesy is currency in Lyon too; one extra word at the table warms the room.

items.meaning: Hello — the mandatory first word of every exchange
Please — add it to the end of your order
Cheers! — the pots are raised to this
That was delicious! — the most useful sentence in Lyon; it wins the patron's heart
